title: A natural experiment in economics - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A new paper by Rohner, Vanden Eynde and Widmer uses the early-2025 publication of a U.S. government 'blacklist' of flagged words as a natural experiment and finds economists at federal-funding-dependent universities sharply cut their use of those words relative to less dependent U.S. institutions and UK scholars, with the drop concentrated in gender, race and environment content and reflected in actual paper content, not just wording. Tyler Cowen accepts part of the authors' 'Science under threat' framing but reads much of the effect as 'removing incentives for pandering.'

insights.claim: The early-2025 publication of a U.S. government list of flagged words functions as a clean natural experiment for measuring how academics respond to political pressure.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A reusable identification strategy for pricing how fast institutions bend to state signalling — applicable to corporate disclosure language as well as academic output.
insights.quote: we exploit a natural experiment: the publication in early 2025 of a “blacklist” of words flagged by the U.S. government
insights.locator: To study whether and how academics respond

insights.claim: Release of the flagged-word list produced a sharp reduction in use of those words among economists at universities that rely heavily on federal funding, relative both to scholars at less federally dependent institutions and to UK-based scholars.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Funding dependence, not ideology, is the transmission channel for political pressure — a screen for which institutions will shift output fastest under policy change.
insights.locator: We find that the release of this list led to a sharp reduction

insights.claim: The measured drop in flagged-word use is driven by content related to gender, race and the environment.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Identifies exactly which research streams — including ESG and climate-adjacent economics — face supply contraction under federal funding pressure.
insights.locator: The drop is driven by content related to gender, race, and environment

insights.claim: The authors show the changes are not simply semantic relabeling but reflect actual shifts in paper content, meaning research agendas moved rather than just vocabulary.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Rules out the benign 'they just renamed things' interpretation, so the effect on the stock of published evidence in these areas is real.
insights.quote: We show that changes are not simply semantic but reflect actual paper content
insights.locator: We show that changes are not simply semantic

insights.claim: Neither individual funding status nor time-invariant author characteristics drive the effect, pointing to institutional-level exposure to federal money as the operative mechanism.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Anticipatory institutional caution spreads to researchers who take no federal money themselves — the chilling effect is broader than the grant recipients.
insights.locator: neither the individual funding status nor time-invariant author characteristics

insights.claim: The paper documents heterogeneous effects by department quality and by author gender and ethnicity.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Suggests the adjustment burden falls unevenly, which is where the follow-on political fight over research funding will concentrate.
insights.locator: We also document interesting heterogeneous effects

insights.claim: Cowen partly accepts the authors' 'Science under threat' framing but argues a large share of the observed behavior change is better described as removing incentives for pandering rather than as suppression of science.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: The same dataset supports two opposite narratives about U.S. research quality — expect both to be cited in the funding-policy fight, so discount headline framings.
insights.quote: I do see some of that in operation, but I also see a lot of “removing incentives for pandering.”
insights.locator: I should note that the authors frame their results

insights.claim: Cowen explicitly leaves the weighting between suppression and de-pandering to the reader, declining to assert a single interpretation of the measured effect.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Signals genuine interpretive uncertainty — treat claims that the evidence settles the politicization debate as overreach.
insights.quote: Your own weights here may vary.
insights.locator: Your own weights here may vary.

insights.claim: The findings are read by the authors as evidence that scholars respond strongly to political pressure, a behavioral elasticity that appeared within months of a mere published word list with no formal enforcement described.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Soft signalling from government moves institutional behavior quickly and cheaply — relevant to how fast regulated industries pre-comply with unlegislated policy signals.
insights.quote: Our findings are consistent with the idea that scholars respond strongly to political pressure.
insights.locator: Our findings are consistent with the idea
